doc.title: Tim Ries interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 19, 2022

title: Motivation for diverse projects; how the Jazz Griots began on a flight
summary: Ries says he does not think about money; a chance seat-mate on a flight to L.A. led to meeting a film director.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: So the diverse things you’ve done in your career, I had mentioned earlier on these three videos, and you went from “Jazz Griots” [scats] that lick in there; and then the gypsy band from Budapest; then to trading licks with a flamenco dancer. Are these projects and

directions simply the product of your big ears, your curiosity, or are they sometimes directed by economics, what’s happening in the business now? I mean what goes into these projects, which I imagine are never easy — I want to assemble this group of people and do this particular kind of music?

It’s never easy and I don’t ever think about the money part of it. And I probably should if I was more wise that way I would maybe get a lot more money but all of the projects are just like this is what I want to do and somehow I’m going to make it happen somehow, like the “Jazz Griots” is just like this project with Jordan Walker-Pearlman and he’s a film director in L.A. And only because I was on a flight going from New York to L.A. I was sitting next to a gentleman who is a producer and he’s a lawyer but he’s also a film producer. So he finds interesting projects to do. And he actually did a really amazing film called “Equal Means Equal” about women’s rights. And he’s just one of these incredible humans that like — and ironically I was sitting in my seat on the aisle and it was like one of those things right before the door shut I thought great, I’m going to have a whole row to myself to L.A. Right before the door shut this guy comes in with his son and they sit next to me. But I was actually wearing this hat, and you know he goes, “Oh that’s a really cool hat.” I said, “Oh well thank you.” So anyway that started the conversation and he goes, “Oh I like hats.” I said, “You want to try it on?” Anyway he said, “I’ve never worn that —” anyway, that started the conversation. “What do you do?” I didn’t even talk about the Rolling Stones, I’m a musician. Anyway well I’m going all the way to L.A. talking the whole flight and he was like, “Well I’m actually producing a film and we’re doing this, we’re showing it for the first time out.” He says, “Why don’t you come to the film?” I said, “Well I’m doing a recording so I can’t.” “Oh, well here’s my card” and it turns out our houses were near each other. “Let’s have lunch when we get back.” “Okay cool.” So now we’re leaving the airplane, “Well have fun.” So now we’re waiting for our bags to come off the turnstile. Now L.A. is huge, right? So then we’re like okay, “Where are you going? Well what’s your hotel? Well I’m staying at this hotel. Wait a minute, you’re at the same hotel?” Now I’m staying at this hotel because it’s two blocks away from the recording studio, Capitol Studios and they have that famous round building where Frank Sinatra recorded and even The Beatles. So for me it was convenient. For him he was way on the other side and he was like oh I just picked it ‘cause it looked like an interesting hotel. So I’m like wow. I said, “Look I have to go there, we’ll share the taxi.” Now we’re talking again. Then I get to meet his wife who is meeting him at the hotel, so we had breakfast. It was like, then it became like because I had this connection with him I told him about my idea for the “Jazz Griots.” He goes, “I think that sounds really interesting.
